items.title: Earth's core may be leaking a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
items.snippet: Scientists have discovered an unusual carbon signature in Hawaiian volcanic rocks that suggests some of Earth's carbon originated in ancient meteorites and later escaped from deep within the planet's core. The discovery raises an astonishing possibility: Carbon essential to life may have traveled from space to Earth's depths before emerging through volcanoes billions of years later.

items.title: Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history
items.snippet: Earth’s journey from an oxygen-starved world to a planet capable of supporting complex life may have unfolded very differently than scientists once believed. A new analysis suggests that oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere in three major stages, with the oceans taking millions or even hundreds of millions of years to catch up.

items.title: Ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side rewrite the Solar System’s violent past
items.snippet: Scientists studying ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side have uncovered surprising evidence that challenges decades of thinking about the Solar System’s violent past. Instead of a single catastrophic bombardment, asteroid impacts appear to have declined gradually over billions of years, revealing new clues about Earth's early evolution and the origins of life.

items.title: Researchers reveal inner-core structural evolution of Typhoon Bavi using multisensor satellite observations
items.snippet: Tropical cyclones frequently undergo rapid, complex structural changes within their inner cores, such as eyewall replacement and wind-field expansion, that strongly influence typhoon intensity and coastal hazards. However, capturing these multilayered transformations continuously from the ocean surface to the upper cloud tops remains a major observational challenge.

items.title: DNA at nuclear edges forms protective UV shield in developing roundworm embryos
items.snippet: Inside the cell nucleus, DNA is arranged into neighborhoods, some of which are tightly packed and mostly inactive. This so-called heterochromatin typically associates with the nuclear lamina, a meshwork lining the inside of the nuclear envelope. This arrangement helps organize the genome and regulate gene activity. But how and when it forms during embryonic development has remained unclear.
